p: Sadashivrao Bhau was born on 4 August 1730 at Satara into a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family, the son of Chimaji Appa, younger brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and Rakhmabai of the Pethe family. His mother died when he was about a month old and his father when he was ten, and he was raised by his grandmother Radhabai and his aunt Kashibai. He served as a finance minister during the reign of the Maratha ruler Rajaram II.

His first campaign was in Karnataka in 1746. He won his first battle at Ajra, south of Kolhapur, and took thirty-six parganas. In a later Carnatic campaign he conquered territory from the Nawab of Savanur and put down the revolt of Yamaji Shivdev.

Having seen the effect of artillery and light guns in British hands, he built similar units for the Maratha army. In 1760 he engaged Ibrahim Khan Gardi, a former officer of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who brought 2,500 trained soldiers and fifteen cannons. Within two years the infantry and artillery division had grown to 10,000 men and 56 guns.

Appointed to lead the army to Delhi against Ahmad Shah Abdali, he set out from Patdur on 14 March 1760 with about 55,000 men and roughly 200,000 non-combatants, including families and pilgrims. Unlike Malharrao Holkar and Raghunathrao he did not know the politics of the north. He disregarded the advice of Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, to leave the civilians at Agra. The army took Delhi on 2 August 1760 and then stormed the fort of Kunjpura, killing its entire garrison.

Abdali crossed the swollen Yamuna at Baghpat between 23 and 25 October 1760, surprised the Marathas and cut their supply lines. A two-month blockade near Panipat brought famine to the camp, where many civilians and animals died. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas tried to break out. After his nephew Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's heir, was killed around 2 p.m., Sadashivrao reportedly left his elephant and charged on horseback; the empty howdah led some troops to think him dead. He died fighting, and the remaining civilians were massacred. Some records say his headless body was recovered three days later, others that it was never found.

His widow Parvatibai, who had accompanied the campaign, refused the conventional life of widowhood. Around 1770 a man appeared in Pune claiming to be Sadashivrao; he was exposed and became known as Totayaa, the impostor. The Sadashiv Peth quarter of Pune is named after him.

notes: The article dates the second Carnatic campaign (Savanur, Kittur, Badami ...) to 1760, the same year as Udgir and the march north, which looks wrong; I wrote 'a later Carnatic campaign' without a year.
The article gives 10,000 infantry with '50 artillery pieces' in one place and '56 guns' in another; I used 56 (from its artillery section).
The article says the army 'reached Delhi on 1 August 1760, taking the city the next day'; I wrote 2 August.

Abdali's army is given as 45,000 and the camp's non-combatants as roughly 100,000 by November (against 200,000 at the start); I left the second figure out as the article does not explain the difference.
The existing description calls him cousin of Balaji Baji Rao; the article says nephew of Baji Rao I, which agrees.
